newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt detains Shi'ites for forming illegal group.
newsitem.headline: Egypt detains Shi'ites for forming illegal group.

text.p: The Egyptian authorities ordered 45 members of a Shi'ite group detained for 15 more days on Thursday on charges of belonging to an illegal organisation trying to spread seditious ideas, public prosecutor Hisham Suraya said.
He said they would stay in custody pending a court hearing, for which a date has not yet been set.
The 45 Shi'ites were part of a group of 56 arrested for questioning last month on suspicion of trying to recruit followers to promote Iranian ideas in the country.
Public prosecutors are treating the other 11 people as a separate group but they also remain in custody.
Suraya told reporters an investigation showed that the 45 belonged to the mainstream Ithna Ashari or Twelver branch of Shi'ism, the sect of Islam dominant in Iran.
Shi'ism is not illegal in overwhelmingly Sunni Egypt but the government is wary of any Iranian religious influence.
Suraya said that one man, Hussein Ali Derghami, told investigators he had formed groups in five provinces, Cairo, Dahaklia, Sharkia, Giza and Gharbia, to spread Shi'ite ideas.
He said another man, Mohammad Ahmed Abu Alaa, was responsible for propagating Shi'ite thought in eastern provinces, and for distributing Shi'ite books and cassettes.

They are accused of "belonging to an illegal group with aims including subverting the constitution, preventing authorities from enforcing it, harming national unity and social order, and exploiting religion by spoken and written propaganda of fundamentalist ideas and seditious influence."
The government uses much the same charges when it cracks down on the Moslem Brotherhood, a large and influential Sunni organisation outlawed more than 40 years ago.
The Cairo government has regarded Iran with suspicion ever since the Islamic revolution there in 1979 and has often accused Iran of trying to export its brand of Islam.
It says Iran has financed and supported the Islamist militants fighting the police in the south of Egypt. About 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict since 1992.

The Shi'ites differ with the Sunnis originally over who should have led the Moslem community on the death of the Prophet Mohammad. Many differences over doctrine, religious law and political organisation have since developed.
